REUTERS/Alaa Al-Marjani TPX IMAGES OF THE DAYIran-backed Kataib Hezbollah has moved military equipment and established new positions in western Iraq for a possible renewed US-Iran war, while retaining its strongholds despite a government withdrawal order, according to Iraqi media and US think tanks.

Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported on Wednesday, citing informed sources, that Kataib Hezbollah had transferred large quantities of military equipment to western Iraq and established new military positions.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the Critical Threats Project (CTP) said in a separate report that Iran-backed Iraqi militias had threatened and reportedly drawn up plans in recent weeks to attack US assets if the United States and Israel resumed strikes on Iran.

Esmail Qaani, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force, traveled to Baghdad last week and held talks with senior Iraqi militia leaders in an effort to defuse tensions between Kataib Hezbollah and the Iraqi government.

A senior member of Iraq’s Iran-backed Badr Organization previously told Iraqi Kurdish media that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Qaani had reached a written draft agreement to redeploy some Kataib Hezbollah forces to western Anbar province, ISW-CTP said.

The institutes also assessed that Iran-backed Iraqi militias were almost certainly behind drone surveillance of the US Embassy in Baghdad in October, describing it as an attempt to deter Washington from striking Iran.

Militia retains control of Jurf al-Sakhar

Iraqi government security forces had not entered the core areas controlled by Kataib Hezbollah in Jurf al-Sakhar, five days after Iraqi forces began deploying to the area, Al-Mada reported.

The militia had received fresh reinforcements, while Iranian and Houthi advisers remained in the area, according to the report.

The newspaper said the Iraqi army’s deployment had been limited and that federal police had merely reorganized their existing presence without taking control of additional territory.

Zaidi last week ordered Kataib Hezbollah to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakhar, which the militia has controlled since 2014, after Iraqi officials accused the group of operating an oil-smuggling network that diverted hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state-owned oil.

Kataib Hezbollah denied the allegations, describing them as part of a campaign to force it to surrender its weapons.

Iraqi security forces began deploying to the area on Friday under a negotiated compromise aimed at averting an armed confrontation. Under the agreement, Kataib Hezbollah fighters were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq.

Militia fighters integrated into state forces

More than 2,000 Kataib Hezbollah members have been incorporated into the militia-affiliated 72nd and 79th brigades of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), according to Al-Mada.

Previously paid directly by the militia, the fighters will now receive state-funded salaries and benefit from official institutional protection, the sources told Al-Mada.

ISW-CTP said integrating the fighters into the PMF did not reduce the threat they posed to US interests, arguing that brigades controlled by Iran-backed Iraqi militias answer to Tehran rather than the Iraqi prime minister.

The institutes assessed that the integration may be part of Zaidi’s efforts to balance US demands for the disarmament of militias with Kataib Hezbollah’s insistence on retaining its weapons.

Designated a terrorist organization by the United States, Kataib Hezbollah is among Iran’s most powerful militia allies in Iraq and has resisted calls to disarm amid mounting US pressure on Baghdad to bring armed factions under state control.

The group is among several Iraqi militias that have claimed attacks on US forces in Persian Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The combative rhetoric came as US officials claimed their blockade and sanctions campaign had brought Iranian oil exports to a standstill, depriving Tehran of a vital source of revenue.

Hassan Hassanzadeh, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in Greater Tehran, said Iran's defense, missile and drone capabilities were “increasing day by day.”

“If the United States and Israel make another mistake, they will witness the unveiling of new targets, weapons and offensive plans,” he said.

Iran also directed its warnings at Arab countries in the Persian Gulf, accusing several of knowingly facilitating US and Israeli attacks by providing access to their territory, airspace, military facilities and logistical resources.

Iran's representative to the United Nations said those countries were legally obliged to compensate Tehran fully for the resulting damage.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that Iran had exhausted its floating oil stocks and failed to load a single tanker since Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August.

“The Iranian regime is a sinking ship,” Bessent wrote on X, adding that Iran “doesn’t have a drop of oil on the water left to sell.”

The economic pressure has also been reflected in Iran's currency, which fell to another record low on Tuesday, with the dollar reaching 2.856 million rials on Tehran's open market after Washington imposed fresh sanctions on Iranian financial networks.

But Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said statements by American military commanders showed Washington was struggling to sustain the blockade.

He predicted that military exhaustion and mounting financial costs would force the United States to abandon its blockade and withdraw its forces from the region.

Mohebbi, however, said Washington would soon discover that its blockade was futile. He said Iran's armed forces remained fully prepared in equipment, resources and morale.

Meanwhile, China urged Washington and Tehran to keep the door to negotiations open, with Beijing's ambassador to Iran, Cong Peiwu, saying Wednesday that de-escalation and a return to talks should be the immediate priorities.

Cong said China supported a diplomatic settlement of the nuclear dispute and efforts to reach a comprehensive agreement over the Strait of Hormuz.

Listen to this article100%Workers aboard the Indian-flagged tanker Desh Garima as it unloads crude oil at a terminal in Mumbai, India, after passing through the Strait of Hormuz, April 30, 2026. (Reuters)Oil exports from Persian Gulf producers outside Iran have nearly returned to prewar levels despite attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates surpassing their prewar crude and condensate export volumes, Kpler data show.

Across the Persian Gulf, producers outside Iran had nearly restored prewar export volumes, helped by the diversion of oil through pipelines.

Their combined exports averaged just under 14 million barrels a day in September and October, compared with 14 million before the war. Kuwait and Qatar remained below their prewar levels, Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude oil analysis at Kpler, told Iran International.

The recovery contrasts with the sharp decline in Iran’s own oil exports, with the US naval blockade effectively halting its main crude trade with China, according to maritime sanctions expert Charlie Brown.

“We see the market pay more attention to fundamentals now than to headlines,” Falakshahi said.

Why November’s figures could rise

Kpler’s preliminary November estimate fell to about 12 million barrels a day. Falakshahi said tracking data for the most recent seven to 10 days tend to undercount shipments, meaning the November figure could be revised upward.

One reason is that more ships are crossing Hormuz with their tracking signals switched off, said Iman Nasseri, senior vice president for the Middle East and Asia at FGE NexantECA.

“Traffic might not have necessarily dropped but the behavior of the vessels and ship owners have changed,” Nasseri told Iran International.

Tracking firms can identify additional cargoes later, including when oil is loaded onto other vessels outside the strait. Nasseri said estimates for the first half of November had already been revised upward by more than 3 million barrels a day. He said he expected further revisions in December as more cargoes were identified.

Crude is in surplus while fuel supplies remain tight

Energy analysts who spoke to Iran International estimated that the global crude market was already in surplus by roughly 1 million to 2 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter.

Falakshahi said the global crude surplus could average around 2 million barrels a day in 2027 if export flows hold up. Without a fresh escalation, he saw little room for crude prices to rise.

Nasseri estimated that around 12 million barrels a day of oil had continued to flow through Hormuz since September, including roughly 10 million barrels a day of crude.

Refined product exports through the strait were running at about 1.5 million to 2 million barrels a day, down from around 5 million before the war.

Lower product exports and weaker refinery activity have kept diesel and jet fuel prices above prewar levels, he said.

Tehran threatens tighter restrictions

Iranian army chief Amir Hatami ordered tighter restrictions on shipping through Hormuz until Washington meets Tehran’s demands.

He warned that renewed US strikes would draw a more severe response that could extend beyond the region. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf also said Tehran was prepared to use military means to break the blockade.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Tuesday that Tehran was determined to break the US naval blockade and would respond with full force to any renewed attack. In a post on X, he called the Trump administration’s blockade plans “delusional and futile.”

The warnings followed remarks by US President Donald Trump on Sunday that strikes could resume after the new year if no deal was reached. Trump also warned that Iranian vessels attempting to breach the blockade would be sunk.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Tuesday that three vessels had been struck by unidentified projectiles while sailing east through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. All three continued their journeys, and all crew members were accounted for.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed three tankers caught fire after hitting mines despite US protection. The Joint Maritime Information Center said claims of tankers hitting mines were unconfirmed.

How Gulf exporters kept oil moving

The UAE was among the first countries to coordinate tanker convoys with the United States, Falakshahi said.

Charlie Brown, a senior adviser to United Against Nuclear Iran who focuses on maritime sanctions enforcement and illicit shipping, said Persian Gulf countries found shipowners willing to sail and took on some of the insurance risk themselves. US military support helped vessels get through, he said.
